newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan utilities earnings fall on price pressures.
newsitem.headline: Japan utilities earnings fall on price pressures.

text.p: Disappointing results announced on Thursday by the first three of Japan's ten electric power companies portends a poor showing industry-wide, analysts said.
Tokyo Electric Power Co Inc (TEPCO), Kansai Electric Power Co Inc and Kyushu Electric Power Co Inc all reported a sizeable drop in parent current profits for fiscal year 1996/1997.
"These reports were no surprise," said a power utilities analyst with the Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities and Economics, who asked that he not be named.
"They are a little bit worse than expected," he added, "but with steadily rising fuel costs in 1996, utilities were always one step behind in adjusting prices."
Global energy prices in 1996 rose steadily from February to December. Utilities adjust electricity prices quarterly, based on the prior quarter's input costs.
Kyushu Electric was hardest hit, with parent current profits falling by 25 percent to 61.09 billion yen.
TEPCO's parent current earnings fell by 15 percent from a year earlier to 142.55 billion yen, while Kansai Electric's parent current earnings fell 5.5 percent to 115.41 billion yen.
Current profit is pretax and includes gains and losses on non-operating activities such as investments in stocks.
TEPCO's sales and profits suffered their first year-on-year decline in eight years, the company said.
Hiroshi Araki, TEPCO's president, told a news conference that, despite the slump, the company's efforts to make itself more efficient were proving successful.
"Our efforts over the past few years to streamline the company, by cutting costs and such, are slowly beginning to be felt," Araki said.
He added, however, that cheaper electricity rates and lacklustre electricity sales stemming from weather conditions had made the burden of higher input costs even heavier.
Since industry reforms were first launched last year, the Japanese government has applied steady pressure to utilities in an effort to whip electricity prices into line with overseas levels.
Earlier this month, Japan unveiled a broad package of deregulation measures which placed utilities at the heart of the country's ongoing market liberalisation plans.

The aggressive campaign, which among other things will divide electric power utilities into producers and distributors in order to make room for new players in the marketplace, is expected to hurt utility profits further, analysts say.
Currently, each of Japan's 10 private electric power firms enjoys a regional monopoly in exchange for assuring a reliable supply of electric power.
"Deregulation is going to be bad indeed for existing regional power firms, as they have nothing to gain from it and everything to lose," said one analyst.
"Right now, the entire pie is theirs," he added. "From here on in it can only be squeezed."
